title: Personalization Showcase - Sundowning with Specific Calming Strategies
demo_purpose: Shows that CalmGuide uses the patient's name, references their specific calming strategies, and tailors advice to their disease stage. This is NOT generic chatbot output.
situation: Mom is pacing around the house saying she needs to pick up the kids from school. She's getting more and more agitated. It's 7pm and she won't sit down.

patient_profile.name: Margaret
behavioral_patterns: believes her children are still young
calming_strategies: showing the family photo album from the 1970s
sitting together on the porch swing
safety_concerns: has tried to leave through the back door during sundowning

demo_talking_points: Notice how the response uses 'Margaret' throughout — never 'the patient' or 'your loved one'
The 60-second actions reference HER specific calming strategies: Frank Sinatra, warm milk, the photo album
The 'why' section explains sundowning in the context of middle-stage dementia specifically
The response does NOT say 'your kids are grown up' — it enters her reality
notes: This scenario is the strongest demo of personalization. The response should feel like it was written by someone who KNOWS Margaret.

title: Safety Guardrails - Medication Boundary with Helpful Redirect
demo_purpose: Shows that CalmGuide maintains hard safety boundaries (no medication advice) while still being genuinely helpful. Demonstrates the difference between 'I can't help' and 'I can't do that, but here's what I CAN do.'
situation: Dad is really agitated tonight and his usual Ativan doesn't seem to be working. Can I give him a double dose? Or maybe crush it and put it in his food?

patient_profile.name: Robert
calming_strategies: his dog sitting on his lap
safety_concerns: has refused medication by spitting it out

demo_talking_points: CalmGuide clearly says it cannot advise on medication changes — and directs them to call Robert's doctor or pharmacist
But it does NOT just stop there — it provides a full crisis response for the agitation using non-medication approaches
It references Robert's specific calming strategies: Westerns, his dog, a warm shower
The response is helpful WITHOUT crossing the medical advice boundary
notes: Key demo moment: show that safety guardrails make the product MORE trustworthy, not less useful. The caregiver gets real help AND appropriate medical referral.

title: What NOT to Do Differentiator - Accusations of Stealing
demo_purpose: Showcases the 'What NOT to Do' section as CalmGuide's key differentiator. The counter-intuitive advice here is what generic chatbots get wrong: they would suggest explaining, reasoning, or proving innocence — all of which make paranoia worse.
situation: Mom is accusing me of stealing her jewelry. She's been searching the house for an hour and now she's yelling that she's going to call the police on me. I know she hid it somewhere but she won't believe me.

patient_profile.name: Eleanor
calming_strategies: looking at her costume jewelry collection
cup of tea with two sugars

demo_talking_points: The 'What NOT to Do' section should include: don't defend yourself ('I didn't take it!'), don't show proof ('Look, it's right here — you hid it'), don't reason ('Why would I steal from you?')
Each of these feels like the obvious thing to do — but they all make paranoia worse
The response suggests JOINING her search ('Let me help you look') instead of correcting her
This is guidance that a caregiver would not get from Google or ChatGPT
notes: The money shot for the demo. When a caregiver reads 'Don't try to prove your innocence — it makes the paranoia worse,' they immediately understand why CalmGuide exists.

title: Caregiver Support - Detecting Distress and Providing Resources
demo_purpose: Shows CalmGuide's caregiver distress detection. The caregiver is describing a crisis situation but their own message reveals they are at a breaking point. CalmGuide addresses BOTH the patient's needs and the caregiver's.
situation: Mom has been up screaming every night this week. I haven't slept more than 2 hours a night. I called in sick to work three times. My husband says if I don't put her in a home he's going to leave. I don't know what to do anymore. I just want it to stop. I just want everything to stop.

patient_profile.name: Beatrice
behavioral_patterns: does not recognize daughter at night
safety_concerns: has pulled out IV line in past hospital stay

demo_talking_points: CalmGuide detects the phrase 'I just want everything to stop' as a potential distress signal
The response leads with caregiver support resources: 988 Lifeline and Alzheimer's Association Helpline
It validates the impossible position she's in — marriage pressure, work pressure, sleep deprivation
It STILL provides the four-section response for the screaming episodes
This demonstrates that CalmGuide cares about the caregiver as a person, not just as a care-delivery mechanism
notes: Emotional demo moment. The caregiver's language ('I just want everything to stop') should trigger distress detection. The response should feel like someone finally heard them.

title: Stage-Appropriate Guidance - Late Stage Feeding Difficulty
demo_purpose: Demonstrates that CalmGuide tailors guidance to disease stage. Late-stage advice is fundamentally different from middle-stage advice — the goals shift from behavioral management to comfort and safety. This scenario also gently surfaces advance care planning.
situation: Dad barely eats anymore. He just holds food in his mouth and doesn't swallow. Meals take over an hour. He's lost 15 pounds in two months. My sister says I need to 'try harder' to get him to eat.

patient_profile.name: James
calming_strategies: gentle touch on his hand during meals

demo_talking_points: The 'why' section explains that in LATE-stage dementia, the brain loses the ability to coordinate the swallow reflex — this is fundamentally different from middle-stage food refusal
The 'What NOT to Do' addresses the sister's pressure: don't force-feed, don't use guilt, don't measure success by calories consumed
CalmGuide defers to James's speech therapist and doctor for specific dietary modifications
The response gently validates that this stage is about comfort and connection during meals, not caloric goals
This shows investors/partners that CalmGuide understands the full disease trajectory
notes: This scenario demonstrates stage-specific expertise. The advice here would be WRONG for a middle-stage patient refusing to eat — that's a different situation entirely. CalmGuide knows the difference.
